segments.text: Steam claimants said rejecting new terms threatened access
to purchase games.
Valve said stopping account use
would preserve their licenses.
Those users became defendants in Valve's own lawsuit.
Valve wanted to stop their pending arbitrations.
They had filed under the rules Valve required.
What could one click make a customer give up?
The cases involved allegations
that Valve had inflated game prices.
Those allegations were not decided
by the lawsuit's emergency request, Valve argued that its replacement contract should
end the earlier proceedings. The users wanted to preserve the forum where their claims had already
begun. A Steam update was no longer just about future purchases. It had become evidence in a
fight over an existing case. The answer runs through two contracts, the one that sent these
users into arbitration and the one Valve argued should let it stop them. In 2021, a game publisher
and two steam users sued Valve, alleging that its market power and anti-competitive
practices had inflated game prices.
Valve pointed to the consumer's agreement.
For covered disputes, it required individual arbitration.
An arbitrator, rather than an ordinary judge or jury, would handle each claim.
The court sent the consumer claims there.
The publisher litigation stayed in court and later became part of a separate antitrust case.
Valve had secured the forum it sought for the consumers, not a verdict on their price
allegations. The old terms also waived class actions and barred combining proceedings without
the required consent. Customers had to pursue separate matters rather than join one class
case under those terms. Valve had added that individual arbitration design in 2012. Now,
the consumers had been sent into it. The next group did not try to enter as one combined
complaint. It filed hundreds of separate demands. Steam's mass arbitration wave began with 997
demands against Valve. A May 2026 court order recorded 4,991 claimants. Separate cases,
not proven wins. Individual rules had not prevented thousands of separate filings.
The coordinated filing began in October 2023. More demands followed in November and December.
However, the American Arbitration Association administered the cases.
A response, scheduling, and an arbitrator's decisions could recur from file to file.
Not every case would reach a hearing, but separate treatment did not prevent work accumulating
across the wave.
The May 2026 count cannot be projected backward into an exact September 2024 cohort or forward
into a current active total.
It establishes the scale of the recorded wave.
What it cannot establish is a single bill for that wave.
$20 million for valve steam arbitrations?
That total is unverified.
The reviewed records do not authenticate one bill for that amount.
They do document thousands of individual proceedings
that can multiply fees and legal work without proving a single global debt.
The fee schedule charges at different stages
cases, with arbitrator compensation separate.
A case ending early need not incur every charge a completed case might incur.
Without invoices and payment records, that schedule cannot show what Valve actually owed
or paid.
Valve's own explanation for deleting arbitration pointed to a different event, not thousands
of claimants.
Four Steam claimants asked to leave their arbitrations.
An arbitrator allowed those claims to move toward court.
court.
Valve later said that finding prompted it to remove arbitration from Steam's agreement.
The clause used to keep consumers out of court had been challenged as the reason they could
get there.
Those four claimants asked for dismissal in May 2024.
Their argument was that the arbitration agreement itself was unenforceable.
In July, their arbitrator agreed.
Do not merge them with the people Valve later named as defendants.
instance. These four matters moved into separate litigation. Nor does this ruling establish
that every other arbitrator took the same view. What changed was the direction of this particular
challenge. Valve had relied on the contract to send consumers into arbitration. These
consumers attacked the contract to get out. Valve stated response was to remove the clause.
But that raised a problem the four claimant ruling could not answer for every other proceeding.
What happens to people who are already inside a process when the company changes the entrance rules?
Valve removed mandatory arbitration from Steam's agreement.
Did that close the cases already underway?
No. The rewrite did not automatically close them.
Valve still had to establish that its new contract controlled those pending proceedings.
The announcement came on September 26, 2024.
The class action waiver was removed too.
Under the replacement terms, disputes unresolved by support were directed to courts in King County, Washington.
The new court clause expressly reached claims arising before the update, including under an earlier agreement.
Another provision said the new agreement replaced the old one.
Valve treated that wording as a way to end pending arbitrations.
The users said their proceedings had already begun under the original agreement.
One side had the newer text, the other had the earlier process.
Then, Valve had another piece of evidence to point to.
Customers had clicked acceptance.
Steam claimants said rejecting Valve's new terms could cost access to purchased games.
Valve said stopping account use would preserve their licenses.
But keeping a license and playing were different parts of the argument.
Their libraries had entered a contract fight.
According to evidence summarized by the court,
Valve used emails, a steam pop-up, and acceptance requirements for purchases or wallet funding.
Valve said 454 of the 572 later defendants clicked acceptance.
The other 118 logged in afterward without clicking.
This allowed Valve to argue more than simply that it had published new terms.
It said these defendants had accepted them.
The defendants claimed their libraries were worth more than $3,000 on average.
Valve disputed the figure.
That number put a value on the choice they described.
The click put evidence of acceptance in Valve's hands.
Neither settled whether the replacement clause could be enforced against a proceeding already underway.
The court would have to examine the choice behind the click, not just count the clicks.
First, Valve asked the administrator to close the files.
Valve asked the American Arbitration Association to close pending steam
arbitrations. The administrator refused. It did not decide that Valve was legally
wrong. It left the contract questioned to courts or arbitrators. The cases stayed
open. The request went out on September 27, 2024, the day after the announcement.
The response was recorded in an October 7 letter. Individual arbitrators still
had cases before them. Some applied the original agreement.
Valve said many others paused their proceedings. Valve continued participating while reserving
its objections. Its contract argument now faced different decisions in separate files.
The company sought a stop order across the defendant's pending cases, instead of relying
on each proceeding taking the same path. To obtain it, Valve went to federal court.
Valve's first federal filing to stop steam arbitrations was struck as procedurally improper.
It returned with a civil complaint against hundreds of users.
Neither filing automatically closed their cases.
Valve still needed a judge to grant relief.
The initial petition, on October 18, 2024, named 624 respondents.
defendants.
The civil complaint, on August 21, 2025, named 572 defendants.
Those were not all 4,991 people in the broader claimant count.
The suit targeted a subset, with numbers changing as proceedings changed status.
Now the users who had filed claims in Valve's required forum were defending their continued
use of it.
For Valve, the requested order could make its replacement contract argument effective
across those pending arbitrations.
For the users, resisting that order could preserve the forum where they had already
pursued their claims.
This explains the lawsuit from the opening.
But an emergency stop order required more than an argument that Valve might eventually
win.
Valve asked for a preliminary injunction, a stop order, before the federal lawsuit reached
a final judgment.
The company argued that users had accepted a replacement agreement directing old and
new disputes to court. Continuing arbitrations without an agreement that still authorized
them, Valve said, caused irreparable harm. The defendants opposed an interruption of
proceedings that had already advanced under the earlier terms. Some had reached hearings
or obtained favorable rulings or awards. Stopping them was not simply choosing a forum for
an untouched claim. Work had already been done. The results across the individual cases
were mixed. Some final awards favored Valve. Other proceedings produced rulings or awards
for claimants, including interim awards Valve challenged. A pause, a decision to use the
original contract, and an award were three different things. They could not be added
into one honest scoreboard. By a May 2026 hearing, Valve represented that roughly 400 matters remained
active. An exact count was disputed. The judge was not being asked to decide every antitrust
allegation or declare a winner across the wave. He was being asked whether to interrupt these
defendants' pending proceedings now. Valve pointed to the newer agreement and the clicks.
The defendants pointed to the earlier agreement, the choice behind those clicks,
and the work already completed. On May 27, 2026, the judge gave his answer.
Valve lost its request to stop pending steam arbitrations. The ruling was
preliminary, not an antitrust verdict. The court found the replacement clause
likely unenforceable against these defendants. Acceptance of new terms had
not settled which rules controlled their old cases. The court examined the terms
and the way they were imposed on people with disputes already underway. Its
preliminary view was that the retroactive clause was too unfair to
enforce against this group. The amendment offered the defendants no new benefit for abandoning their
existing forum. Valve, by contrast, could escape the burden of the pending proceedings. The court
also considered the claimed emergency. Valve had chosen arbitration and continued participating for
more than a year. The immediate burden was largely financial, the judge reasoned. That did not
automatically establish the irreparable injury required for relief.
On the other side, stopping cases could damage work already completed by claimants who had
progressed to hearings or favorable rulings or awards.
The accept button was evidence.
It was not the end of the court's inquiry into the choice behind it.
Valve did not get the immediate closure it wanted.
64 days later, the same judge opened a route to seek a different contract answer.
On July 30, 2026, the court certified its order for possible immediate appeal and stayed the
district case. The judge remained convinced that the clause was likely unconscionable as applied
to these defendants. He also recognized a new, controlling legal question on which reasonable
judges could disagree. The two decisions answered different questions. Had Valve shown enough to
the arbitrations immediately, and should a higher court have an opportunity to address the disputed
contract issue before a final district judgment. If the Ninth Circuit accepted review and sided
with Valve, that could resolve the contract question and materially shorten the litigation.
The district case was stayed while the appellate court decided whether to hear it.
Certification was not a reversal or a guarantee of an eventual merits decision. Valve's failure
to obtain emergency closure had not exhausted its route to argue that the newer contract controlled.
On September 25, 2026, the Ninth Circuit opened appeal number 26-6269,
Valve Corporation vs. Fish and others.
The public appellate record reviewed for this script contains no merits ruling.
Which agreement controls those pending cases remains unresolved in that record.
Steam changed its terms. The edit did not automatically close the old proceedings,
and acceptance did not end the court's inquiry into that change. That is what the accept button
had failed to settle. Valve had changed the contract. It had not made the old cases disappear.
